segments.text: Hi, and welcome to today's iPhone Duo Group Lab.
Thanks for joining.
I'm Curt, a technology
evangelist on Apple's Worldwide Developer Relations team.
My colleagues and I will be taking your questions for the next hour.
If you're watching on the Apple Developer site,
please submit your questions in the panel on your right.
If you're watching on YouTube and would like to submit questions or vote
for your favorites, please hit the link below.
The Worldwide Developer Relations team has been hosting workshops around
the world to help developers get ready for iPhone Duo.
Developers have also been posting about the work they've
been doing using Xcode 27.1 and Device Hub.
We've been so impressed by everyone's efforts to get their apps
ready. Just ten days until iPhone Duo is in people's hands.
I'm super excited about our panel for this Group Lab.
You all come from a variety of different backgrounds and you worked
on different things. And one of the things I find so cool
about iPhone Duo is how the team
came together to produce this really amazing product.
And so maybe I think it would be good that we kick off by letting
you each introduce yourself and say a little bit about what you worked
on in this product. Nathan. Well, I'm Nate,
I worked on the design team for the Duo,
so mainly on the overall way the system fits together:
Home Screen, Lock Screen, multitasking apps.
Pinned video, those sorts of features.
Yeah. Great.
I'm Grant, I'm a human interface designer at Apple,
and I worked on features for the iPhone Duo, including a whole
bunch of the apps. So things like Messages, Files, Measure,
and a bunch more of the apps on iPhone Duo.
Hi, I'm Andy and I'm an engineer on the UI frameworks team
for the Duo. I worked on various components,
getting them ready for the Duo environment,
including tab bars, menus and various other components.
Hi, I'm Anna. I'm also on the UI frameworks team,
and I got to work
a lot with all of these folks on the vertical bar
and other features on iPhone Duo.
I mostly work on bars and then navigation within apps,
so stuff like NavigationStack or TabView.
Awesome. So excited for the panel
and with the breadth of expertise that we have.
So we've got some questions
that have come in. And so we'll,
we'll dive in.
So this first one is,
is an initial design question.
So the question is how should developers approach designing
an app that feels native across different iPhone poses.
And I think we'll start with you on this one, Grant.
Different poses. Rather than simply
adjusting an existing phone's layout to the larger display.
Yeah, I think the key thing to remember is that you're making one app
for the iPhone, whether it's an iPhone Duo
or the iPhone Pro or any other kind of iPhone, right?
And so you want your app experience to be fairly
consistent across all the different poses and all the different layouts
that it can show up in, right? So you want the same,
usually the same type of controls or a similar set of controls,
the same kind of hierarchy, the same kind of navigation and all
that kind of stuff. And you want it to be continuous as you move between it.
So people know where to look for controls. They know where everything
is and they know how it all works.
Yeah. And so I think that's the place to start: this is one app
you're creating and it just shows up in different poses.
And maybe some of the controls show up vertically.
They show up horizontally, but they're still the same controls and it's
still the same app that should feel the same across the different devices.
Sure. Nate, do you have anything to add to that? Well, I think that kind
of covers it. I think the unique thing about this phone specifically
is people will use it in a lot more orientations.
It's very, I don't know,
it's handy, like place it down, prop it up.
So in that way, within a single phone,
your app's going to get used in a lot more.
Yeah. States than you might for just other phones.
But yeah, taking advantage
of the layouts across the full lineup, I think is key.
Yeah. This is my experience when I get to play with one.
And unlike some of our panelists, I'm not carrying one.
But my experience, I wonder if you echoed this,
is it's an object that is nice to hold and manipulate
and to use as a physical thing.
And so I think that's one of the fun things about it.
And I think people will very frequently move between poses.
Absolutely. Yeah.
All right.
Our next question is about
the hinge and positioning views.
So Andy, I'm gonna start with you on this one.
Sure. So when repositioning a custom view to avoid
the partial fold division region, what guidance do you
have to choose which side of the screen it should move to?
Left. Right. Top. Bottom.
An example is the favorites added in library
pop-ups in Music. Is there anything we should think about in terms
of making those decisions?
Yeah. So I think in general,
there's a lot of different ways, different views
that could avoid either way. But I think for a lot of them,
we tend to avoid more to the right because we found that more people
are more likely to hold it that way. And so some
of our views gravitate for controls more towards the right.
But then also there's other elements
that are maybe smaller and it,
you would almost want to avoid it towards the side
that it is mostly on if it was between the two.
So one example of this is context menus.
And the edit menu for text editing is that we will tend
to stay on the side that the source view is on.
So if you know your cursor
is currently on the left side, we will actually bring
up the menu will stay on the left side so that it doesn't feel
like as you're holding the device, it just shifts all the way to the other
side and doesn't really have that continuity anymore with the source
view it came out of. And I think that's how we've been approaching it.
And I think that's worked a lot for us.
Yeah, I think this is something that the hierarchy of your app can also
really drive. And the way that Andy is saying, you often end up
with app layouts that have a primary and a detail layout
that ends up horizontally and at least on the left-to-right language,
you often end up with the primary on the left and the detail on the right.
And so that drives the decision of how it avoids the fold.
Is that just from your the hierarchy and the visual hierarchy of your app
and the structure of it, like things are already placed in an appropriate
position, and then they can just shift over to avoid
the fold in that way.
One other thing that's worth really considering
is when the device is posed or is placed seated.
And so you have a part
that's flat on the ground and then a part that's upwards.
It can be really useful to keep the interactive
controls closer to the bottom. And that can really help
with making sure that there's a stable surface to press against for that.
Right. Thinking about our first question
and moving between different arrangements of the device,
are there considerations around what goes
when the phone's open, what goes on the right side
in order for it to still be there when someone closes the device?
Is that something we should think about too?
I think that will happen automatically in a lot of cases. So if you
have a primary and a detailed layout, oftentimes that detail
will be the thing that you see when the device closes as well.
And so it's often keeping the content fixed
or relative to what it is.
But that almost, in many ways, works automatically because the detail
is the furthest down the hierarchy. And that's
where you say when you close the device as well. That makes sense.
I guess we actually see that in the two center shots of Mail.
Behind.
Here. So. Excellent.
All right,
I'm going to throw this one at you. Anna. I haven't read the whole
question, but it starts out with GeometryReader near the top.
All right. I think it's going to be technical.
And it just jumped away from me. Here we go.
Apps using a custom
two-pane split with GeometryReader.
After rotating the unfolded
Duo from landscape back to upright in the Simulator,
a pane kept its landscape width
until we stopped a child view.
This gets.
Let me try to summarize.
So they're using a custom two-pane
split with GeometryReader, and they're seeing some
problems on rotation and opening and closing.
And would we recommend
that they try moving to ArrangementView.
For this. Yeah, I think there's
various details in here that are probably relevant.
So if you haven't heard about them,
there's ArrangementViews,
which you can style to be a split arrangement
and something that I think is super cool about that is your,
you can customize that ratio of the columns.
And in a lot of cases that can
eliminate things that you might have previously been using
a GeometryReader for. And that's something
that works on Duo, but it also will work on other iPhones.
So that can be pretty powerful.
But I would say in general, if the GeometryReader is reporting a width
or a size that you are not expecting on rotation,
that would definitely be worth filing Feedback for sure.
All right.
This is an interesting question, and I.
Nate, I'm going to throw it to you.
I think we may all
want to chime in or maybe none of us will.
So the question is,
do we actually need a physical iPhone Duo to test
or can we test in the Simulator?
Will keeping a physical iPhone Duo be better for testing
than the Simulator?
If yes or no, why?
That's a good question.
No, you don't need a physical iPhone Duo to test.
There's lots of ways you can test.
You can even test some of the features that are relevant to iPhone Duo
and other iPhones.
But specifically for the Duo, there is a great
Simulator experience that you can use to end-to-end
test your app in all of the different states and poses.
And it's really helpful.
Like any other iPhone,
there are very specific things that you might not be able
to test on a device.
Like if you're a camera app, for example,
there might be some features of camera streaming that are better on a phone.
Or if you need to deal with more complicated APIs
that are hardware-specific, but your average app
can be fully tested in the Simulator.
Anybody have anything to add to that? I would also say that I think
there's also some things that can come up around the design
of your app and how does it feel on an actual
iPhone Duo versus in the Simulator, right? Are there things where,
when you're holding it in your hands, the placement
of controls or the structure that you choose for your app?
You might make different decisions on a physical device than you might make
in the Simulator, right? And that can happen with any kind of device, right?
There's lots of different ways to do it.
Yeah, I remember that when the watch first came out, it's
like everything I built was way too small until I actually got a watch.
Exactly, exactly. And so I think from that perspective,
it can be very valuable
to try things out on an actual iPhone Duo.
But from the other perspective, I think for the vast majority of things,
being able to see it in iPhone Simulator will give you a huge amount
of insight into how it behaves, how it works
in the different orientations and different layouts of iPhone Duo.
And so from that perspective,
I think it is a great way to test out your app. And I don't think
that unless you're doing very specific physical Arrangements, that you can't
get a feel for or simulate that you're probably pretty
well off with what you're seeing in the Simulator. And it's a good sense
of how it feels. Anna Andy, anything to add?
No, I think,
I think I just echo both Nate and Grant.
The Simulator is great.
It does. There is a lot more flexibility,
compared to simulators for other phones. This really allows
you to go between the different states and let you try different things.
And you also you can get inspiration from just looking
through system container APIs and how
they adapt on the Duo. And then that can, that you can then use
that to make your own decisions on how you want your app to adapt.
Yeah. And that's an important
point to acknowledge the Simulator that's in the betas
right now doesn't have most of the first-party apps in it.
It's a limited set
until release of the device in just ten days.
Soon. Soon? Yes. Very soon.
No, I think I would just echo those points. I would say honestly,
as someone who has access to using a device
and using a Simulator, I still find that I am doing a good
amount of my work in the Simulator just because it's
more convenient or yeah, things along those lines.
Excellent.
Let's see. The next question is about StandBy.
I think I'll start with you on this one, Nate.
Will developers be able to make use
of the screen space available
with the new StandBy experience through Live Activities.
And sorry, the question moved on me.
Through Live Activities, the newly selectable widget sizes.
And then we'll stop there, because the rest
of the question is forward-looking and we can't answer it.
Yeah, absolutely.
So all the different sizes of widgets that we support
in StandBy for other phones directly translate to the Duo.
We've introduced a new,
I can't remember what it's called in the developer documentation, but it's
an extra large, essentially.
I think that's what it's... I think you call it extra large.
And basically fills
like half of the Duo screen when it's open.
So that's a great new widget format to support,
not just for the Duo, but for other devices too.
So they will work.
And in terms of Live Activities,
one of the great things about the Duo
is if you do have it in the book configuration,
you can have your time and date and calendar on one side
and then a Live Activity open on the other side
so you can have it showing music. If you're listening to music,
if you've got a flight coming up, you can show the flight,
you can pin it open there. Or whatever your app comes up with.
Yeah. So yeah, so whatever your app does
in its Live Activity, that would be useful for someone on the lock screen.
That'll also translate into the StandBy experience when it's open.
That's awesome. Yeah, it's really great.
Cool.
This is an interesting one. I'm gonna start with you on this, Andy.
Ultimately it's a camera question.
And so I might weigh in as well,
but it's also about how the device is being
held on iPhone Duo should camera apps think of opening
and closing the device mainly as a camera direction change
or more broadly, as an adaptive layout transition?
I'm not sure I have the best
answer for that, but I would have to take that one.
Okay. Yeah. So I think if you're a camera app,
the act of opening the phone
is more likely to be keep the cameras where they were.
So rear-facing, for example,
if you're a photography app and then the customer probably
just wants more screen real estate to see
that through that camera view
in the case where you're using the front-facing camera,
so you're in, say, a video calling app,
then I think opening,
there's this assumption that the front-facing camera is still relevant.
So there is going to be the switch
from the closed display camera to the internal camera.
And that should happen automatically if you're using the right APIs. Right?
Yeah, yeah. It's super important if you're making
a camera app to use the AVCaptureDevice RotationCoordinator
and DirectionCoordinator to follow that.
In the past, apps have been able to keep track of the size
of the display and orientation and figure out those things.
The variety of poses on iPhone Duo mean
that you really need to be using
AVCaptureDevice RotationCoordinator
and DirectionCoordinator. So if you're not, please do.
Yeah. One other thing just about camera apps.
Since I worked on a few of them
that not directly about the question, but it could be useful
information to think about is when the iPhone Duo is open,
the camera on the back is still a portrait aspect ratio, right?
But the screen is in a landscape aspect ratio.
And this is one of those things that the aspect or the
orientation coordinator that you were talking about really helps with,
but you have this choice at that point: do you want
to show a portrait preview inside of the landscape screen with
letterboxing, or do you want to zoom it up and fill the screen with it?
Right. And that's a choice that's really up to your app, what you
think is best for the use case of your app, right? The way we
thought about it for our apps is that for really photography-type use cases
of the camera, it can be good to show the full camera sensor preview.
And that's why you'll see in the camera app. The default is the
camera preview is center frame.
It's framed there. But in other experiences, like AR
or augmented reality experiences, things like ARKit,
we went edge to edge and zoomed in that camera preview to fill
the screen because it's less about the highest-quality
exact camera frames and more about the interactive experience
that you're having using that kind of stuff.
It's not exactly about the question, but I thought it might be interesting.
I think there's another piece to it.
I think we got at the camera aspects of it.
Well, but it is also an adaptive
layout transition. If the size of the view is changing,
you have to adapt to that. And so it's not an either or.
It's a both.
For sure.
Let's see. This question
has been upvoted. So I feel like we need to address it,
but I'm afraid I can't actually answer it.
So the question is, will Simulator gain additional apps like Photos
and Files so we can discover how they behave in different poses
and make our app match those expectations?
I appreciate your willingness to and desire to make the app match
the things we're doing.
I'm afraid until the updates are released,
we can't talk about future events
or releases, so I can't give you a direct answer.
But stay tuned.
I'm going to start this one with you,
Anna, and you can throw it down the line if you want.
I spoke to someone who got to try interacting with the Duo
at an in-person session.
They mentioned that in the tabletop pose,
the seated pose, that tapping
or interacting with the top half could tip the phone over.
How do we think about this and other physical aspects of design
and interaction with apps?
Yeah. I can probably speak to this as someone who is more using it,
and then I might throw it down the line for the folks who
have been thinking about this more than me,
but I would say,
quite frankly,
it is a, it's sturdier than you would expect.
I really can interact with it
and it's not going to tip over.
But just like Grant said before,
placing controls where you may be really using
them frequently on the bottom can not only be good from a
device position perspective, in terms
of the hinge, but also just from a reachability standpoint,
if the device is like this, it's closer for me to go here
than it is to go up.
And you can rest your wrist on the...
Yeah, yeah.
Yeah. And adding to that too, I think. Something to think
about is, yeah, you want to keep your controls at the bottom because it's
just easier to interact with that, but also
trust your users because I think they'll gravitate towards the best way
to use your app as you go based on different experiences.
So one big example is in your video playing app,
the controls shift down to the bottom while your video stays
at the top because you're now seated farther away
to watch this video. But if you're in an app where somebody
is more needing to interact with it more, they might not choose
to put that in the seated position because they might just actually want
to be reading something and they would be scrolling, and it might just feel
better holding the device in their hand or having it lie flat.
And I think that's depending on the experience you're
going for. What really matters is which pose you want them to focus on,
rather than to say, "I need to do every single one,"
because I think you can trust your users to gravitate
towards the experience that best fits your app. And that's some
of the magic of iPhone Duo is you have all of these different
layouts and poses
and states and everything available to you, and you can pick which one
is appropriate for the experience you're using. And I think
to pick, I would say there are three things to weigh up.
If there is primary content, like a video,
you probably want that included. So shifting the controls
to the bottom makes a lot of sense.
There are benefits just from interacting
on the tabletop surface that could make sense for your app.
But then the third thing to consider is we try to avoid having
controls move significantly when you go between poses,
because it just feels very, I don't know,
it feels very drastic sometimes in the video case.
It feels like it makes a lot of sense because it's helpful.
There are examples where moving a button can feel very unhelpful.
And so it's just not worth that movement.
So I think keeping an eye on keeping
yourself in check on the moving is a good thing too.
But with hinges too,
or when you're avoiding a particular region like that movement. Also,
I don't know how you think about what maybe should or shouldn't avoid,
but it seems like that's also a movement question.
Yeah. Being yeah, being mindful of too much movement.
I think start with as little as possible, unless there's
enough value that it's worth it in that new pose.
Yeah.
All right. Great.
I love this question and it's a design question at heart,
but I think everyone might have an interesting take on it.
So we'll start with Nate and see where we go.
For developers with an existing iPhone-only app,
what are the top three things we should fix first?
So it feels great on iPhone Duo
unfolded display without a full redesign,
but let's just say so it feels great on iPhone Duo,
and you don't all have to come up with three. Maybe between the group we come
up with three. But then we can argue about the priority
of those or something. That's a good question, I think.
When you run your app in the Simulator and you just build
against the new SDK and you just see how your app looks,
there's going to be some very obvious things
that you can fix that are very easy to fix.
And then suddenly your app will just feel native.
We're seeing people build for the new SDK already.
So we're seeing apps show up and it's, and the translation
to the Duo is really natural for a lot of apps.
So I think minimal amount of work and it's going to look
and feel great. And then beyond that, I think there are ways
you can take advantage of the extra screen real estate,
specifically the width when you're in landscape.
And I think there it's thinking about, for this view,
is there an auxiliary view that would make sense beside it,
or is there a primary,
secondary relationship in
the hierarchy of my app.
Would that make sense? So then reaching for the split
views and the ArrangementViews and looking at it as two
halves of a book might make sense,
but I do think you can start with the first
step of just like making sure your controls are laying out vertically
and making sure your content
just doesn't stretch too wide, like lines of text
being across the full width of the screen will look a little bit wonky.
Yeah, that's one thing we've seen in the workshops,
once folks get the controls on the side
and they're using the full real estate.
Sometimes it just feels a little stretched.
Yeah. See how to chunk that.
We have this concept of readable content width,
and you don't want to make texts really, really long,
or it's painful to read. So I think if you, if you think
through that mindset of staying within a comfortable reading
width, then you'll notice when there's room for something else.
And that's when you can start to layer in the other pieces.
Yeah. I agree with that. I think number
one is adjusting for the asymmetric safe area and making sure
that you don't have content that's going under horizontal safe areas
or hard to reach or totally impossible to access.
I think number two is making sure that you have the right controls showing up
in the vertical layout of the toolbars and navigation bars.
So making sure that you don't have controls that are showing up without
icons or showing up
without have text labels, even though it would be better off with an icon
or other things like that and making sure that's right. And then I think
the third point is what Nate said about having
readable content margins
and taking advantage of that, whether you're just adding additional margin
in those landscape poses so things aren't too wide to read
or you're finding additional
columns to show or whatever you decide is appropriate for your app.
But I think that would be the order I would think about.
Andy, Anna, any favorite bugs
that show up a lot and people need to fix.
I wouldn't say bugs, but I think, piggybacking off the same
idea is I won't attempt to prioritize this,
but I think a lot of iPhone-only apps generally
start with that singular NavigationStack hierarchy.
And I think starting to think about
taking advantage of that space, maybe switching to more of a
NavigationSplitView so that you can show more of your hierarchy,
like Mail, where when there's not a lot of space, when you're
in that more compact environment, you do just push the environment through.
But as you get more space, you can now show your message list
and you can also show your message detail at the same time.
And some of the things that we've seen apps
do in our workshops as well is traditionally
iPhone widths have been more narrow. And so a lot of people,
when they have horizontal carousels, they make assumptions about,
let's just use the device width, subtracting, maybe some padding.
And that's how much each row should look like.
I think there's looking at that and seeing if there's
a better heuristic on maybe capping to some aspect ratio,
or maybe just reducing, so that now you just get a better horizontal
scrolling experience so that as this device gets wider,
your screen space gets wider.
Instead of just enlarging
the content, you now just surface more content to the app.
Because a lot of times that's what I'm, how I'm using my phone is,
when it's closed, I'm just quickly glancing through something.
But if I really want to take advantage of that space, I just open it up
so I can now just see more of the app. And that's something
that we've been recommending a lot of people in our workshops.
Yeah. Great call. Anything?
Yeah. No, definitely. If you've been assuming,
especially if you've been locking to portrait only,
that is something where your app may have a good amount of assumptions
that you just didn't know because you never were testing
it in those ratios.
I think I would also say
that considering if you can go from a standalone bar
to using the system container managed
bars is another just good thing to consider for general
bar hygiene, but particularly on the Duo.
The system is only able to move bar contents vertically if you're
using those system containers. So in SwiftUI that's NavigationStack,
NavigationSplitView, TabView, and in UIKit,
UINavigationController, UISplitViewController. Same thing.
Instead of using a UIToolbar
and then positioning it yourself,
or at the very least auditing it and making sure
that is an intentional decision, that it is staying horizontal. And I think
it's worth a lot. Some people don't know that UINavigationController also
supports toolbar items at the bottom,
and those are the ones you want to use. And so if you have a
custom UIToolbar
and you also have a UINavigationController, oftentimes
the toolbar items are just available for you right there.
And you can get the system and behavior quite easily.
Yeah, yeah. I think one of the unique things, well, one of the new
things about this device is on previous
on other phones,
I think developers can expect that they own
the whole bottom edge, or they own the whole top edge,
and that's their place to put custom controls.
That doesn't translate super well to the Duo because the
side controls share the space with the status bar in both
portrait and landscape when it's open. And so now you're having
to play in the same space as the system. And it becomes
a lot more burdensome to support all the different states.
So moving to those system components that are automatically going to get
out of the way of the status bar. And when there's a Live Activity coming
and going, how are you going to resize and move out of the way
becomes even more important
to stand on the shoulders of the APIs.
Yeah. And being prepared to handle getting
a vertical safe area, which this is something that you might have already
been getting if you're using a NavigationSplitView.
But if this is your first time getting to have this sidebar,
then that's a new thing to adapt to.
Another thing that you mentioned auditing Anna
We've seen a fair number
of folks with an overflow menu inside their overflow menu.
Oh, yes. So if you're doing
a custom overflow menu on your own, there are APIs
to add those items to the system overflow menu. And then
when the system needs to overflow more, they're all in one spot.
So the bar video that Anna
and Maria did talks about that API.
The other thing I would say is, this is something that's
just more obvious on Duo than it is on other phones:
if you're using a custom view in your toolbar items.
That's something that's a lot more obvious in some ways,
because the system isn't able to move that to be vertical
automatically, because it doesn't know how wide
it needs to be, if it will be able to fit the fixed width of the bar.
And so if you're using a custom view for something that's
effectively an image, I would consider, if you can just set
the image on the item and let the system handle it for you.
Same thing for custom back buttons.
Yeah. There is also
a way you can set it to go into the vertical axis anyway, right?
Yeah. So there's a,
the Axis behavior API where you can say that it prefers vertical.
One other thing that we've found in workshops, when you say prefers
vertical, it doesn't mean it will go vertical on other phones.
It will still stay horizontal. So you can set that and you don't
need to do anything that's conditional to do it.
You can just set it. And then
the system will look at the runtime conditions and figure it out for you.
Great. Good to know.
So the next question is about testing.
And I'm going to throw
this one to you because we've talked about it.
We run automated UI test suites in CI.
And currently there are no UIDevice or simctl APIs
to change the hinge state
and orientation doesn't rotate the Duo Simulator.
Are official APIs planned?
We can't talk to future plans, but any recommendations
on what folks should do in this situation.
Yeah. First, if the hooks are the things you want to test
aren't exposed, file Feedback so that they get exposed.
But I would say just in general, thinking about testing,
as an engineer, what are the cases that I need to be thinking about?
Because also often when I've been developing, say, for iPhone
and then I run my code on iPad, I'm like, this looks completely broken
because I wasn't testing or thinking about it.
